picks.title: Valley English learners made academic gains this year. How a new law will help them continue succeeding
picks.take: Three Central Valley districts report about half of their ELs moving up a level on California's English proficiency test. Merced credits having classroom teachers give the test to their own students, so they see what it demands and plan practice for it. A new state law also drops teacher and parent sign-off as a reclassification hurdle.
picks.try: Ask your EL specialist what ELPT tasks look like, then build one speaking or writing prompt in that format into this week's lesson.

picks.title: Amid Immigration Crackdown, Let's Support School Family Liaisons
picks.take: A Boston University researcher argues that family liaisons and front-office staff, not policy, are what make immigrant families trust a school: they explain EL services, find rides and food, and hear deportation fears. She found liaisons part-time, without devices or private space, paid far below teachers. Most Mississippi schools have no liaison, so that work lands on EL teachers.
picks.try: Find out who at your school a newcomer parent actually calls, and put that name and number on your syllabus in the home language.

picks.title: 'Teacher as Participant' and Other Methods to Engage English Learners
picks.take: Four veteran EL educators each name one strategy: mini-whiteboards for whole-class answers, sentence frames with the same idea repeated in talk and writing, screen-free card and bingo games for vocabulary, and previewing the five to ten words a unit really needs. The common thread is low-stakes, high-participation practice any content teacher can run without a separate EL curriculum.
picks.try: Model your own answer to a discussion prompt aloud, slip in one deliberate error, and let students catch it before they write theirs.
